Experimental cohorts of the fairy shrimp Streptocephalus torvicornis raised under controlled laboratory conditions at a constant water temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C] provided detailed data on early developmental milestones. Newly hatched nauplii measured approximately 0.1 cm [Lb = approximately 0.1 cm] in total body length at birth, reached at an age of 5.06 days [ab = 5.06 days] since fertilisation, which is a modest size typical of anostracan crustaceans emerging from su at a temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C]bitaneous eggs. The process of yolk absorption and the onset of phytoplankton grazing occurred within the first several days post-hatch, as the free-swimming nauplius larvae began actively filtering suspended particles from the water column. This initial size places Streptocephalus torvicornis well within the range reported for other species in the genus Streptocephalus, though the value is comparatively small when set against the ultimate lengths achieved later in ontogeny. Such a diminutive body length at birth reflects the substantial degree of post-embryonic growth that must occur before the individuals can progress through critical life-history transitions, including sexual maturation and eventual reproduction. The duration of these early, yolk-dependent stages is tightly coupled to the ambient thermal regime, and under the isothermal conditions applied here, development proceeded at a predictable and consistent rate across all replicate rearing vessels.

As development progressed, the growing juveniles exhibited a steady increase in body dimensions, culminating in a maximum recorded total length of 2.5 cm [Li = 2.5 cm] for fully grown adults. This ultimate total length, which represents the asymptotic body size attained after the conclusion of the most rapid growth phase, was consistently observed among mature individuals that had completed their final series of moulting events, a size that aligns closely with values reported for Streptocephalus similis and other medium-sized anostracans inhabiting similar temporary pools in subtropical regions. The post-metamorphic juvenile phase, during which the exoskeleton is periodically shed through successive ecdysis events, is the period of most pronounced somatic expansion, with the body length nearly doubling between the onset of exogenous feeding and the approach of puberty. Attaining this ultimate length requires that the individuals maintain high ingestion rates and efficiently convert ingested algae and detritus into new tissue, a process that is eventually redirected toward gamete production as the animals approach reproductive maturity under the stable thermal conditions of the experimental setup.

The onset of gonadal maturation was carefully documented by monitoring the development of secondary sexual characteristics and the first appearance of ovigerous females within the experimental populations. At the constant temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C], the time since birth at puberty was recorded as 20 days [tp = 20 days], by which point individuals had reached a total length of 1.3 cm [Lp = 1.3 cm], indicating that female fairy shrimp begin producing their initial clutch of eggs approximately three weeks after emerging from the egg. This value aligns well with the rapid life-history strategy typical of anostracans occupying ephemeral aquatic habitats, where early maturation enables at least one successful reproductive event before the pond dries. The morphological transformation from juvenile to sub-adult—marked by the development of the brood pouch in females and the enlargement of the second antennae in males—was clearly visible by this same developmental milestone, which precedes the attainment of maximum body length. Growth continues for some time even after reproductive activity has commenced, a pattern that contributes to the species' high fecundity under favorable conditions.

Reproductive output was assessed by collecting and counting the eggs released by individual females maintained at 25 °C [T = 25 °C] throughout their adult lives. Observations of single females showed that each clutch typically contained approximately 67 eggs [N_R_i = each clutch typically contained approximately 67 eggs], and females produced roughly one clutch every 36.73 days [F_R_i = roughly one clutch every 36.73 days], resulting in an average daily egg deposition rate that underpins the species' considerable fecundity under favorable thermal conditions. This fecundity value was obtained by monitoring a cohort of breeding individuals housed individually in small containers to prevent egg cannibalism and allow precise enumeration. Each clutch typically contains numerous small, subitaneous eggs that are extruded into the brood pouch and subsequently released into the water column, where they either hatch rapidly or enter a resting stage if conditions become unfavorable. The capacity to generate such a large number of eggs over a relatively short interval is an adaptation to the unpredictable hydroperiod of temporary pools, ensuring that some offspring will encounter suitable conditions for development. The combination of high fecundity per clutch and sustained clutch frequency underscores the ability of Streptocephalus torvicornis to achieve substantial population growth during brief windows of habitat availability.

Longevity under the standard experimental conditions of 25 °C [T = 25 °C] was found to average approximately 120 days [am = approximately 120 days], a lifespan that is characteristic of many short-lived branchiopod crustaceans. This value represents the mean time from hatching to natural mortality across both sexes, although males may persist for considerably longer, with some individuals surviving up to 285 days. The ultimate dry weight of fully grown adult females was measured at 0.0266 grams , a value that reflects both the accumulation of structural tissues and the storage of lipid reserves necessary to support repeated reproductive bouts. This dry weight was obtained by collecting mature individuals, drying them to constant mass at 60 °C, and weighing them on a microbalance, providing a reliable estimate of the species' maximal somatic mass, which is modest even among anostracans and falls within the range of 0.02–0.03 grams reported for Streptocephalus species of comparable body length. The relatively modest dry weight, combined with the short lifespan, reinforces the rapid life-history strategy of this species, which prioritizes early and prolific reproduction over extended somatic maintenance and growth. Under the experimental thermal regime, physiological death typically followed a period of declining reproductive activity, with females ceasing egg production several days before succumbing to senescence, a pattern that places Streptocephalus torvicornis among the more rapidly cycling members of the Anostraca, finely tuned to the demands of its transient freshwater habitat.
